raw_text:
Wallen Introduces Legislation to Strengthen Tick-Borne Disease Tracking
September 23, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Catherine Wallen (R-Adams/Cumberland) introduced
House Bill 2710
aimed at improving Pennsylvania’s ability to track tick-borne diseases and ensuring medical professionals have up-to-date information to diagnose and treat them.
“As someone who lives with Lyme disease, I know firsthand the challenges that come with a tick-borne illness,” Wallen said. “What can begin with a tick bite can lead to months, years and sometimes a lifetime of symptoms, doctor visits and uncertainty. Unfortunately, my story is not unique.”
While Lyme disease is the most recognized tick-borne illness, other diseases are also a growing concern. Babesiosis, which is transmitted by ticks, is not currently included on Pennsylvania’s list of reportable diseases. The Pennsylvania Department of Health has previously supported adding babesiosis to the state’s reportable disease list. Wallen’s bill would require health care practitioners, facilities and laboratories to report cases to the Department of Health.
“Without accurate reporting, we do not have a complete picture of how widespread these diseases are,” Wallen said. “Requiring babesiosis cases to be reported will give public health officials better data to track the disease and respond appropriately.”
House Bill 2710 also would require medical professionals to complete one hour of continuing education focused on tick-borne disease diagnosis and treatment as part of their initial licensure and renewal requirements.
Wallen said action is needed to improve disease surveillance while also giving health care providers the tools they need to recognize tick-borne illnesses.
“If we are serious about addressing the growing threat of tick-borne diseases, we need better data and better education. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can make a significant difference for patients,” Wallen said. “Patients deserve timely diagnoses, appropriate treatment and support. This legislation is about making sure Pennsylvania is doing everything it can to provide that.”

“These investments are a great example of how funding can make a real difference in our communities. From replacing aging public safety and public works vehicles to improving water infrastructure, emergency medical services and recreational facilities, these projects address important local needs and strengthen the services residents rely on every day,” Wallen said. “I’m pleased to support this funding and the communities that are putting these dollars to work to improve infrastructure and quality of life for residents.”

Investing in Adams County Agriculture
August 19, 2026
By Rep. Catherine Wallen (R-Abbottstown)
Agriculture is a cornerstone of Adams County’s economy, heritage and future. Keeping our farms and orchards competitive requires more than hard work in the fields. It also means embracing new technology that can improve efficiency, increase production and strengthen the future of Pennsylvania agriculture.
I am pleased several Adams County agricultural businesses and organizations received funding through the Agricultural Innovation Grant Program. The investments will help local operations adopt innovative technologies, protect our soil and water resources, and support the next generation of agriculture.
Among the recipients are Piney Apple Acres ($102,381) for precision harvest technology; Mt. Ridge Farms ($65,800) for a vacuum-assisted automated harvest system; and Rice Fruit Company ($33,160) for an AI-powered smart radio system with real-time translation capabilities for its multilingual workforce.
Other local recipients include Adams County Nursery ($33,800), Fruit Hollow Farms ($12,493), Fairview Dairy Farms ($36,048) and Pennsylvania State University ($14,600), which will evaluate precision spray technology for tree fruit orchards.
Together, these grants represent $298,282 in investments in Adams County agriculture. They will help our agricultural businesses work smarter, operate more efficiently and remain competitive.
Supporting innovation today means protecting the agricultural heritage and economic strength of Adams County for years to come.

“Republicans in the House and Senate successfully pushed back against the governor’s original $53.26 billion proposal, bringing the budget I voted for down to $50.85 billion. That represents a significant reduction from the initial request and spending in the House Democrats’ budget. It also keeps spending growth closer to the increased costs the Commonwealth is already facing.
“I am encouraged that we protected the Rainy Day Fund and avoided broad-based tax increases. I’m also pleased the budget preserves the Educational Improvement Tax Credit and Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit programs without reducing funding or making programmatic changes. These scholarships continue to expand educational opportunities for students and families across the Commonwealth. Also included in the budget is $775 million for shovel-ready rapid deployment rural road and bridge projects.
“While this budget is an improvement over where negotiations began, we must continue working toward budgets that live within our means and put Pennsylvania on a sustainable fiscal path.”
